Harness Leverage Across Model Size: A Ladder of Five Local Agent Harnesses from 0.75B to 4.7B

Journal: Expert Systems with Applications
Hao Wang Corresponding author: Co-corresponding authors who contributed equally to this work.
Email addresses:wanghao994916959@163.com (Hao Wang), huangting6@honor.com (Ting Huang). Affiliation: School of Mathematics and Physics, University of Science and Technology Beijing, Beijing, China    Ting Huang Corresponding author: Co-corresponding authors who contributed equally to this work.
Email addresses:wanghao994916959@163.com (Hao Wang), huangting6@honor.com (Ting Huang). Affiliation: Honor Device Co., Ltd., Beijing, China
Abstract

A harness turns a model into a system that completes tasks: it builds the prompt, exposes tools and decides when work is done. Harness comparisons hold the model fixed. Model comparisons hold the harness fixed. We vary both: five shipped harnesses, 18 artifact-producing tasks, four locally deployable open-weight models from 0.75B to 4.7B and a 35.5B anchor, with one deterministic checker scoring all 360 ladder cells. The completion-controlling harness, Mingbird, has the highest mean at every size. Of four pre-registered paired contrasts, two survive Holm correction, at 0.75B and 4.7B. Thirteen of sixteen paired intervals exclude zero under the deployment reading, with leads from 0.075 over the strongest rival to 0.819 over the weakest. The completion gate is not the carrier: disabling all six executable checks moves the mean by +0.080+0.080, +0.117+0.117, +0.003+0.003 and −0.004-0.004, every interval including zero, and only at 1.9B does disabling it create empty runs. Removing one repeat-blocking rule alone costs 0.411 at 0.75B and leaves eight of eighteen tasks with no artifact. The harness effect is a progress effect: it decides whether a run leaves anything on disk. Of 357 usable cells, 127 leave none of their declared artifacts and 85 of those exit normally, so a scorer that reads exit status credits work that was never written. Whether the effect grows or shrinks with size, four rungs cannot settle: a floor arm produces a rise, a ceiling a decline, and a cross-family rung a peak.

Keywords: 
agent harness , small language models , local inference , task completion , empirical evaluation , resource-constrained deployment

1 Introduction

A local agent is two things at once. One is a language model running on the user’s own hardware. The other is the software around it, which builds the prompt, exposes tools, executes each call, feeds the result back, and decides when the work is finished. In deployed systems this second layer is called the harness, and its components are the ones a cognitive architecture for language agents names: memory, action space and decision procedure (Sumers et al.,, 2024). For a frontier model reached over an API, the harness is largely a convenience. For a model of between 0.75 and 4.7 billion parameters sharing an 8 GB graphics card with its own context window, it can be what decides whether the task is completed at all.

That regime is the one a single consumer card can serve. Small open-weight models fit on such a card with a usable context window, and they are the models that individuals and small teams run. The harnesses those users install were written for a different regime. Two of the four third-party harnesses we test are product-grade tools designed around strong models with reliable tool-call syntax and long, self-correcting reasoning traces. One is a minimal construction kit that trusts the model with four tools. One is a compact bash-only control that assumes the model can hold a shell protocol. A small model breaks these assumptions in different ways, and the resulting failures are not always visible. An agent can end its turn with none of the deliverables written while the process exits normally and the transcript contains no error.

Mingbird was built against those assumptions being false. Its design point is completion control: the harness does not accept the model’s claim that the work is finished until executable checks on the working directory agree. The architecture and the full mechanism set are described in an earlier paper (Wang and Huang,, 2026). This paper measures what that design point is worth, and how the answer depends on the size of the model underneath.

Studies that compare harnesses hold the model fixed, and studies that compare models hold the harness fixed. Neither design answers the question a practitioner with one graphics card faces, which is whether to spend the card on a larger model or on better software around a smaller one. The same trade-off has a name in the scaling literature, where spending more inference compute can substitute for parameters (Snell et al.,, 2024). A harness is the part of that compute a user buys once and reuses. Recent studies do cross the two axes, and they disagree. A pre-registered comparison of three scaffolds on five models found the most capable model gaining the most. A ten-model comparison reports diminishing harness gains as capability rises on issue-repair work and the opposite on open-ended repository work. A seven-scaffold study reports cost differences that widen on a local 27B model, and a three-level comparison on 2–3B models finds that a minimal shell can be worse than raw prompting. None of them holds five shipped harnesses, four locally deployable sizes and one artifact-level scorer fixed at once. Section 2 sets these against each other.

We report a controlled comparison on one machine, one runtime, one task suite, and one scorer. Five harnesses run 18 artifact-producing tasks against four open-weight models from 0.75B to 4.7B, and a 35.5B mixture-of-experts model anchors the top of the range on a six-task subset. Section 3 sets out the cells this runs to, and every cell is scored by a deterministic checker that reads only files in the working directory.

Mingbird has the highest mean at each of the four sizes. Four of the sixteen paired comparisons were registered in advance and enter the Holm family, one against goose at each rung: two survive correction, at 0.75B (adjusted p=0.0067p=0.0067) and 4.7B (0.04100.0410), and two do not. The remaining twelve are descriptive, and thirteen of the sixteen exclude zero under the deployment reading, with leads that run from 0.075 over the strongest rival at 4.7B to 0.819 over the weakest. The advantage is not the completion gate the harness was built around: with all six executable checks switched off, the score moves by +0.080+0.080 at 0.75B and +0.117+0.117 at 1.9B, both intervals including zero, and by nothing at the two larger rungs. The one rung where the gate does its job is 1.9B, where switching it off leaves three of eighteen tasks with no artifact instead of none. The harness changes whether a run ends with any work product. Whether that effect grows or shrinks with model size is a question this ladder cannot settle, and Section 4.3 shows the three measurement artifacts that make an answer look available when it is not.

The decomposition says where the advantage lives. At 0.75B between half and three quarters of each gap is cells the baseline left empty, and most of the remainder is how far a completed run gets. At 1.9B almost all of the gap is availability. Against pi at 4.7B, where no cell is empty, the lead is a depth difference on tasks both arms finish. This design does not decompose that machinery further, but it rules out the completion gate as the carrier at three of the four rungs. The gate is the mechanism the system was built around, and at the fourth rung it does what it was designed to do.

The machinery shows in how runs end. Of 357 usable cells, 127 leave none of their declared artifacts, and 85 of those 127 end with a normal process exit. The rate runs from 6% for Mingbird to 69% for mini-swe-agent. A scoring rule that read the exit status as completion would credit all 85 with work they never wrote, and a harness that reads it that way inherits the model’s stop as a task failure.

Three features of the design set the scope of these claims. An arm whose reply contract no small model meets widens the five-arm span by construction, so the span without it is reported beside the raw one. A scorer ceiling binds at the top, where Mingbird and goose both reach 1.000 on eight of eighteen tasks. And the 3.7B rung is a different model family, so it is read as a deployment point and not as a step on a capability scale. Section 4.3 reports what these features do to the shape of the advantage. One further check runs a single base model at four bit widths from 3.15 to 6.50 bits per weight, because the ladder does not hold quantization constant. It locates where the advantage survives compression and where it does not.

2 Related work

Three bodies of work bear on this study: how agent loops are built and measured, what is already known about harness and scaffold effects, and the resource envelope of local inference.

Agent loops and their benchmarks

The dominant recipe descends from ReAct (Yao et al.,, 2023), in which the model interleaves reasoning with tool calls and the harness executes each call and appends the observation. Practitioner syntheses describe the same loop as a small set of composable patterns (Anthropic,, 2024). Toolformer (Schick et al.,, 2023), Gorilla (Patil et al.,, 2024) and ToolLLM (Qin et al.,, 2023) established learned tool use and reliable API invocation. Reflexion (Shinn et al.,, 2023) and Self-Refine (Madaan et al.,, 2023) improve behavior inside the loop through self-critique, and both presuppose a model that can produce a usable critique of its own attempt. Self-correction without external feedback often fails (Huang et al.,, 2024; Kamoi et al.,, 2024), while CRITIC (Gou et al.,, 2024) shows that supplying tool feedback repairs the loop. That is the design choice behind the completion guards measured here: they execute checks instead of asking the model to introspect (Wang and Huang,, 2026).

Benchmarks for agents span environments and interaction styles. AgentBench (Liu et al., 2024b, ), AgentBoard (Ma et al.,, 2024), WebArena (Zhou et al.,, 2024), OSWorld (Xie et al.,, 2024), SWE-bench (Jimenez et al.,, 2024) and GAIA (Mialon et al.,, 2023) cover browsing, desktops, repositories and open-ended assistance. τ\tau-bench (Yao et al.,, 2025) and τ2\tau^{2}-bench (Barres et al.,, 2025) add a simulated user and verify final database state. AndroidWorld (Rawles et al.,, 2024) and AppWorld (Trivedi et al.,, 2024) move to mobile and application environments. ToolSandbox (Lu et al.,, 2025) and CRMArena (Huang et al.,, 2025) test stateful tool use, and AgentDojo (Debenedetti et al.,, 2024) and CaMeL (Debenedetti et al.,, 2025) add prompt-injection safety. These suites vary the model or the task. The suite used here, LRAB, was introduced in an earlier paper (Wang and Huang,, 2026) and varies the harness on artifact-producing tasks.

Harness and scaffold effects

That the software around a model changes measured performance is established, but its dependence on model size is contested. One line of work names the binding-constraint thesis and calls for mandatory harness disclosure (Zhang et al.,, 2026). A pre-registered three-scaffold, five-model comparison on GAIA finds within-model scaffold effects up to 28 points, and its prediction that better models would be less scaffold-sensitive was rejected in direction: at the harder level the most capable model gained the most (Starace,, 2026). A ten-model comparison of mini-swe-agent and OpenCode reports diminishing harness gains as capability rises on issue-repair benchmarks, with the opposite pattern on open-ended repository work (Hu et al.,, 2026). On the cost side, seven scaffoldings against five models on one fixed software task show that scaffolding dominates cost, with the widest spread on a local 27B model (Alier Forment et al.,, 2026). A theory result points the other way: an inference-time harness can compute a closure its per-call primitive cannot, and the gap closes by enlarging the model, easing the task, or lengthening the chain of thought (Gai et al.,, 2026). That predicts a harness effect that shrinks with size on tasks a larger model can represent directly. One very recent system study reads the balance the other way again: across its traces, task accuracy depends mostly on the model, while harness-side variance moves cost by up to 2.6 times (Park et al.,, 2026). Its measurements come from Claude Code and Codex, harnesses built around frontier models, on software benchmarks. The band below 5B, where a run can end with no file on disk, is the band this paper measures.

Five studies come closest to this one. A comparison of three harness levels on three 2–3B models over 24 tasks reports a non-monotonic result in which a minimal shell can be worse than raw prompting (Cho,, 2026). The ten-model study above covers the capability range and gives the closest evidence on direction. A survey of 66 model-harness configurations, including pi, on frontier models finds model rankings reversing across harnesses (Li et al.,, 2026). A full-factorial comparison of six open-source harnesses and three lightweight coding models over 100 SWE-bench Verified tasks reports resolution rates that differ by up to 44 points across harnesses for one model, rankings that change across models, and more than a 20-fold spread in tokens per resolved task (Zhao et al.,, 2026). The CAIS Arena pins one model across six frameworks on a shared tool server (Milev and Kanagala,, 2026). Our design differs in the band it covers, 0.75B to 4.7B on one consumer card, in scoring declared artifacts rather than test patches, and in a completion-control ablation repeated at four deployment points, which turns a curve into a mechanism.

Two related lines supply mechanisms, not comparisons. Loop detection goes back to the StuckDetector in OpenHands (Wang et al.,, 2024), which normalizes events and counts repeated action-observation and action-error patterns, and the duplicate-call intercept measured in Section 4.5 follows that paradigm. Agentless (Xia et al.,, 2024) shows that a deliberately narrow scaffold can outperform agentic ones on software-engineering tasks, and SWE-agent (Yang et al., 2024b, ) makes the agent-computer interface a design object in its own right. ADAS (Hu et al.,, 2024), AFlow (Zhang et al.,, 2024), GPTSwarm (Zhuge et al.,, 2024) and DSPy (Khattab et al.,, 2023) search harness structure automatically, and AI Agents That Matter (Kapoor et al.,, 2025) argues for cost-controlled evaluation. This study varies whole harnesses, not interfaces, and fixes budgets across arms.

Local inference and small models

llama.cpp (Gerganov and ggml-org contributors,, 2023) established efficient quantized inference on commodity hardware, and Ollama (Ollama contributors,, 2023) packages it behind a serving API. Surveys of small language models (Lu et al.,, 2024) document the latency and memory envelope, and one position paper argues that small models are the future of agentic AI (Belcak et al.,, 2025). SmolLM2 (Ben Allal et al.,, 2025) and the Gemma and Qwen families (Gemma Team,, 2026; Qwen Team,, 2025; Yang et al., 2024a, ) push capability per parameter. Long-context degradation is documented by Lost in the Middle (Liu et al., 2024a, ), Context Rot (Hong et al.,, 2025) and same-task-more-token analyses (Levy et al.,, 2024). Constrained decoding (Willard and Louf,, 2023; Dong et al.,, 2024; Geng et al.,, 2025) targets the tool-call format failures that dominate small-model runs, and format-restriction studies (Tam et al.,, 2024) show the trade-off. Lightweight agent libraries (Hugging Face,, 2026; Open Interpreter contributors,, 2026) make small models drivable with minimal scaffolding, and TinyAgent (Erdogan et al.,, 2024) explores function calling at the edge. The two product harnesses tested here (Block,, 2025; SST team,, 2025) are designed around large-context cloud models and Unix shells, and the two minimal ones (Earendil Works,, 2026; SWE-agent contributors,, 2026) assume a model that can drive a shell unaided. Mingbird starts from the opposite end: 1–9B models, a Windows host, a consumer GPU, and tasks that mix code, files and research. In most empirical work on agent frameworks the harness is a constant. This study makes it the variable.

3 Harnesses, models, and protocol

The study compares five harnesses on one task suite, one scorer, one runtime and one host, across four model sizes. The design is a factorial matrix over models and harnesses, plus a mechanism gradient that repeats one completion-control ablation at four sizes, plus a single upper anchor. It runs to 360 ladder cells, a 216-cell gradient at the same four rungs with a 54-cell repeat of its 3.7B rung, a 72-cell repeat of the ladder’s two decisive rungs, a 36-cell loop-guard ablation at 0.75B, 36 anchor cells of which the twelve on the six-task subset are reported, and a 144-cell precision ladder.

3.1 The completion-controlling harness

Mingbird is a harness written for models in the 1B to 9B range on a Windows host with a consumer GPU. Its architecture, its seven design principles, and its full mechanism set are described in an earlier paper (Wang and Huang,, 2026), and this section states only what the measurements need. A Mingbird run is a plan-execute loop with a typed tool surface, and its distinguishing feature is a completion gate. Before the harness accepts the model’s claim that the work is finished, six executable checks run at completion time: a no-work refusal, a test guard, a finish-claim artifact check, a plan-completeness gate, an artifact-content check, and a post-finish summary request. All six are disabled by AGENT_ABLATION=finish_gate. A seventh, non-executable intervention, a todo-sync reminder, stays on in the full and guards-off arms and is disabled in the text-only arm. A textual re-read of the task stays on in every arm. The gate is the design hypothesis under test: if an agent’s characteristic failure is a normal exit with the work unfinished, then a harness that checks the work instead of trusting the claim should recover part of the loss.

3.2 Models

Four open-weight models span 0.75B to 4.7B, and all four fit entirely in the 8 GB card at the study context. Three come from Qwen3.5 (Qwen Team,, 2026) at 0.75B, 1.9B and 4.7B, which gives a within-family ladder that holds tokenizer and chat template constant. Granite 4.2 at 3.7B (IBM Granite Team,, 2026) is a cross-family anchor. Table 1 lists the parameter counts, architectures, and served quantizations, all read from the served artifacts and not from model names. A 35.5B mixture-of-experts model (Ornith AI,, 2026) with about three billion active parameters anchors the top of the range on a reduced task set. It is an anchor in parameter count and deployment cost, not in measured capability: in the earlier matrix the 4.7B Qwen outscored it over the same eighteen tasks (Wang and Huang,, 2026).

Parameter count does not order capability across families, so a cross-family rung can be weaker than the rung below it. We therefore read the ladder as a set of deployment points, not a capability scale, and the analysis reports the within-family slope alongside the four-rung one for exactly this reason.

3.3 Harnesses

Five harnesses span the design space. Mingbird is the completion-controlling harness of Section 3.1. pi is a minimal, MIT-licensed construction kit with a four-tool loop. OpenCode and goose are product-grade harnesses with native JSON tool calling and different architectures, a client-server product and a protocol broker. mini-swe-agent is the compact bash-only control used in recent harness studies. Table 2 lists versions and the tool-call path of each. Table 3 lists how sampling, thinking, context and the wall budget are enforced for each arm, because those mechanisms differ by harness and are part of the treatment.

The unit of comparison is the harness as shipped, not a prompt written for this study. Each harness brings its own system prompt, tool surface, context policy and completion logic, and that bundle is the artifact a practitioner installs. Holding prompts constant across products would measure a configuration none of them ships and would remove the mechanisms under study. The price is that a difference between two harnesses cannot be attributed to one design decision. The mechanism gradient exists to pay that price, because it switches the completion-control family on and off inside one harness with everything else fixed.

The five harnesses also differ in tool-call protocol. Four pass a structured call from the model to a typed tool. mini-swe-agent drives the shell with text and runs whatever bash block the model writes. The protocol axis is not separable from the arm’s role here, because the only text-driven harness is also the only bash-only control, so we treat the axis as descriptive, not as a factor.

3.4 Tasks and scoring

The task suite is an 18-task held-out set: fifteen workflow tasks (HWF-01–15) and three long-horizon tasks (HLH-01–03). It was frozen before the ladder started and covers four tiers: retrieval over a fixture database (HWF-01–02), synthesis across records (HWF-03–06), multi-step workflows with file edits and checks (HWF-07–15), and long-horizon runs with an intermediate deliverable (HLH-01–03). Each task ships a fixture directory, a prompt, and a deterministic scorer. The scorer reads only files in the working directory and awards partial credit per check. It never reads the agent transcript, so a harness cannot score by describing work it did not do. The scorer’s optional judge dimension is disabled in every reported run. The score is milestones at 4/7 and final artifacts at 3/7. Table 11 in the appendix lists the tasks and the number of checks each carries.

The held-out set mirrors a development set task for task: HWF-01 is a literature-map task where WF-01 is a literature review, HWF-05 a cleaning pipeline where WF-05 is one, and so on. The instances are distinct, with different fixtures, prompts, required artifacts and checks. The families are not distinct, and the design is deliberate: a family-level match lets the ladder ask whether the harness effect depends on model size and not on one particular fixture, while the development cells stay untouched. Every cell reported here is a new run under this protocol.

3.5 Execution protocol

Every arm runs on the same Ollama 0.40.6 server with temperature zero and thinking disabled. Context is pinned at 32K for every arm: Mingbird through AGENT_CTX, with its compaction summarization call at 8000 as Table 3 records, and the four CLI arms, which send no context field, through the server’s OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH default of 32768 fixed at the server restart of 22 October 2026. The loaded model’s processor split and window are recorded from /api/ps at the end of every cell, so a cell that ran partly on the CPU, or against a server whose window was not the protocol’s, can be identified and not merely inferred. The record reaches every scored cell except the first three, whose window rests on the server log rather than on a per-cell snapshot.

The wall budget is set per (task, model) and is identical across harnesses for a given task and model. Each budget is 1.3×1.3\times the maximum wall clock observed for that cell among the completed cells of an earlier collection on the same machine, floored at 10 minutes and capped at 120. Where fewer than three cells of that task and model completed, the per-tier value applies instead, 20 minutes at 0.75B, 30 at 1.9B and 3.7B, and 45 at 4.7B, plus 30 for the long-horizon tasks. A single budget per tier would be wrong in both directions, because the spread across tasks exceeds the spread across models: on granite4.2:3b the maximum completed wall clock is 3.9 minutes on HWF-12 and 50.5 on HLH-03. Within a rung the order of harnesses alternates by task, forward for odd tasks and reverse for even ones, so that warm-up or drift cannot systematically favor one harness.

The 35.5B anchor ran all eighteen tasks at a 45-minute budget per cell and is reported on the six with the fewest final deliverables, ties broken by task id. The budget is set above this model’s observed needs rather than to a round number, and one cell at this rung still reaches the 45-minute limit. Only a quarter of the model’s weights are resident in the card (5.5 of 22.6 GB), so the rung runs mostly on the CPU and its wall clock is not comparable to the ladder’s.

3.6 What the instrument can measure

We report four measurement properties of the suite, all from the collected cells and with no additional runs.

Discrimination. A task separates harnesses at a rung if the five arms do not all land on the same score. At 0.75B, 16 of 18 tasks separate, and two (HLH-02 and HWF-05) return zero for every arm. At 1.9B every task separates, and at 3.7B 17 of 18 do, HWF-01 being zero for every arm. Dead tasks cost nothing in a paired contrast, because they are zeros for every arm, but the nominal 18-task coverage is 16 tasks at the smallest rung.

Reliability. We split the 18 tasks at random into two halves, recompute the five-arm profile on each half, and correlate the two profiles, over 2,000 splits. The median correlation is 0.92 at 0.75B (5th to 95th percentile 0.79 to 0.99), 0.81 at 1.9B (0.50 to 0.97), 0.93 at 3.7B (0.78 to 0.99), and 0.96 at 4.7B (0.86 to 1.00). The ordering is therefore unlikely to be an artifact of which eighteen tasks were drawn. The 1.9B interval is the widest, with a 5th percentile of 0.50, so that rung’s ordering is the least stable of the four.

Parallel forms. The held-out families mirror the development families structurally. Whether they also mirror difficulty is an empirical question. On the same model, across 18 family pairs, the correlation between development and held-out task difficulty is +0.23+0.23 (p=0.36)(p=0.36), and between their discriminating power +0.20+0.20 (p=0.43)(p=0.43). With eighteen pairs the interval around each correlation is wide, roughly ±0.45\pm 0.45. A structurally mirrored family therefore provides no evidence of parallel-form transfer, which is weaker than evidence of absence. We use the match for coverage of the same capability families, not for calibration.

Check-level reach. The suite has 115 distinct (task, artifact, check) keys over 117 check entries. Of these, two are passed by every arm, one is failed by every arm, and the remaining 112 separate at least two arms. The check that no arm passes is a word floor on HWF-09’s benchmark report, which is met in none of the fifteen cells that produce the file, so it is unreachable at this scale rather than informative. The two that carry no information are a substring check on HWF-03’s script and a compile check on one HLH-03 module.

3.7 The mechanism gradient

The matrix shows where the harnesses separate. The gradient asks a narrower question: whether the completion-control family carries Mingbird’s own advantage, and whether that contribution changes with size. The three-arm completion-control ablation is repeated at 0.75B, 1.9B, 3.7B and 4.7B, eighteen tasks per arm. Full runs all six executable checks. Guards off disables all six and keeps the todo-sync reminder and the textual re-read. Text-only disables the six checks and the todo-sync reminder and keeps the textual re-read alone.

Two limits follow from the design. The gradient ablates one harness, so it cannot explain the span across harnesses, which is carried by arms other than Mingbird. The third rung, 3.7B, runs on granite, so it is the ladder’s only cross-family point and is reported as a check rather than entered into the slope, even though the gap to the comparator is smallest there. If the guard contribution is flat across the three same-family rungs, then whatever moves Mingbird’s advantage with size lies outside this family.

3.8 Analysis plan

The unit of analysis is the task. Comparisons use paired task-level bootstrap intervals (10,000 resamples, seed 42; the replication checks of Section 4.2 resample 4,000 times with seed 20261115), the paired sign proportion, and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. Zero differences are discarded, as the signed-rank test requires, and the pp values come from the normal approximation with the tie correction, not from the exact distribution, because the absolute differences are heavily tied within a rung. At 4.7B eight of the eighteen tasks are exact ties, and those pairs drop out of the signed-rank test. Slope intervals resample the 18 tasks inside each rung and refit on log10\log_{10} size.

The comparator for the confirmatory contrasts is goose, fixed before this ladder ran because it was the strongest baseline in the earlier matrix (Wang and Huang,, 2026), and not chosen from this ladder’s results. The confirmatory family has seven tests: the slope of the five-arm span, a shape test on the gap, the slope of the guard contribution, and four per-rung Mingbird-versus-goose contrasts, with Holm correction. The 35.5B anchor is analyzed separately and is not part of the family. Everything else in the paper is descriptive.

The hypotheses and their estimators were fixed before the ladder’s second rung started. The four per-rung contrasts reported here are the ones the family contains. The rescored reading is a second reading of the same cells, applied where a run reached the wall budget with at least one declared artifact on disk. It is not a pre-specified test, and where the two readings disagree the paper reports both.

The minimum detectable effect is not small. With eighteen paired tasks and the observed paired standard deviation, which runs from 0.34 at 4.7B to 0.58 at 3.7B, the design detects a difference of 0.22 to 0.39 at 80% power. The value is reported next to each gap. Repeated collection of one configuration moves an arm mean by up to 0.233 (the matrix and gradient collections differ by 0.233, 0.229, 0.148 and 0.012 at the four rungs, and the two 3.7B gradient collections differ by 0.066), so absolute levels are read with that scale in mind. Paired contrasts are computed within a collection and are not compared across collections. The design is built to detect large effects: a harness that completes a quarter of the tasks and one that completes three quarters.

The scorer cannot tell a document built from the fixture from a plausible one the model invented, so we audit that separately. For every cell whose task has identifier-bearing fixtures, we compute the fraction of record ids and DOIs in its artifacts that appear verbatim in the task’s fixture file as shipped with the suite, and report the complement as the fabricated-identifier rate. The audit does not enter the score. It tells the reader whether a high score came with the right content.

4 Results

Four research questions organize the results. RQ1 asks whether the completion-controlling harness scores above the third-party harnesses at every size. RQ2 asks whether its advantage changes with size. RQ3 asks what part of the harness carries the advantage. RQ4 asks how small models fail. A fifth subsection narrows a caveat that the threats section states rather than answers: the ladder holds the harnesses fixed but not the bit width, and a compression that moves the two arms unequally would be recorded here as an effect of size.

4.1 Score by size

Table 4 reports the mean artifact score for every harness and model, and Figure 1 plots the same means against the measured parameter count. An arm’s mean is taken over the usable cells it has, which is 17 at 0.75B for Mingbird and goose and 17 at 3.7B for Mingbird, and 18 everywhere else.

The ranking is Mingbird first at every rung. At 0.75B the five separate by 0.653, and Mingbird produces every declared artifact on eight of its seventeen tasks against three for pi, two for goose and none for the two smallest harnesses. At 1.9B it leads pi, goose, OpenCode and mini-swe-agent in that order, and completion comes apart from score, since every artifact is present on twelve of its eighteen cells against six for pi and none for mini-swe-agent. At 3.7B pi draws level at the top, and the order below it reshuffles: mini-swe-agent moves from fifth to third while OpenCode falls to last. Artifact production does not track the ranking there either: pi completes fifteen full sets to Mingbird’s fifteen, and two of pi’s complete sets reached the wall budget, so a full set of files and a zero coexist. The paired contrast at that rung is 0.005, and with the pair at 1.9B it is one of only two in the table whose interval includes zero under both readings. At 4.7B every declared artifact is present on seventeen of eighteen Mingbird cells, against thirteen for pi and ten for goose.

The ladder is read across the two axes at once. Mingbird at 0.75B averages 0.664 in the primary collection (17 usable cells), 0.503 in a repeat (14) and 0.431 in the mechanism gradient’s full arm (18), which repeats the same configuration, so its own level moves by 0.23 with nothing changed. The three cell sets differ because only the ladder and its repeat carry the exclusion rule, so these are three measurements of one condition rather than three draws from one sample. Across the whole 6.3-fold range on the card the winning harness gains 0.304. The other four gain between 0.14 and 0.72: pi 0.72, goose 0.53, OpenCode 0.52 and mini-swe-agent 0.14, the last from a floor where its own reply contract rejects the model rather than from a graded capability. The winner’s gain is small because it starts at 0.664 with a third of the scale left, while pi starts at 0.172 with four times the room. The five-arm spread at a fixed size is 0.564 to 0.819.

4.2 Every harness at every size

Table 5 reports the paired contrast between Mingbird and each of the four third-party harnesses at each rung, under both readings of the data. The two readings answer different questions. Under the deployment reading a cell that exhausts its wall budget scores zero, which is what a machine with a fixed overnight schedule experiences. That zero conflates a harness that could not do the task with a harness that did the task but not inside the budget. The second reading takes the archived working directory of each of the 58 cells that ended at the wall budget with artifacts already on disk and rescores it with the same checker. It asks whether the work was there, and it says nothing about whether the work arrived in time.

Thirty-six of the 58 rescored cells are at 3.7B, so the second reading moves that rung more than any other. pi rises there from 0.714 to 0.869 and Mingbird from 0.762 to 0.841, which turns the pair’s 0.005 into −0.020-0.020. goose rises from 0.262 to 0.327, OpenCode from 0.000 to 0.188, and mini-swe-agent from 0.279 to 0.323. At 1.9B the reading lifts pi from 0.409 to 0.552 and Mingbird from 0.593 to 0.732, while goose does not move at 0.372. The two arms move together often enough that the contrast survives.

Under the deployment reading 13 of the sixteen intervals exclude zero. The smallest is the contrast with pi at 4.7B, +0.075+0.075 with a 95% interval of [+0.012,+0.147][+0.012,+0.147], and the largest is the contrast with mini-swe-agent at the same rung, +0.819+0.819 [+0.647,+0.964][+0.647,+0.964]. The three that include zero are all against harnesses that keep their strength at that size: pi at 1.9B (+0.184+0.184, [−0.080,+0.442][-0.080,+0.442]) and at 3.7B (+0.005+0.005, [−0.230,+0.241][-0.230,+0.241]), and goose at 1.9B (+0.221+0.221, [−0.002,+0.436][-0.002,+0.436]). Under the rescored reading 14 of the sixteen exclude zero, and the exceptions are the pairs with pi at 1.9B and 3.7B.

The 3.7B exception has a cost signature. pi’s mean cell at 3.7B takes 8.1 minutes against 5.3 for Mingbird, and its artifact sets there are completed later rather than not at all. A practitioner choosing between the two at that size is trading a score difference that is not distinguishable from zero against a half again as long a run. Under the deployment reading, which is the one that matches a fixed schedule, the slower harness pays for that trade.

The four contrasts against goose are the pre-specified comparisons and form part of a seven-test confirmatory family with Holm correction (Section 3.8). Two survive the correction: the contrast at 0.75B (p=0.0010p=0.0010, adjusted 0.00670.0067) and the one at 4.7B (p=0.0068p=0.0068, adjusted 0.04100.0410). The 3.7B contrast has a raw p=0.016p=0.016 and an adjusted value of 0.080, and the 1.9B contrast does not approach the threshold. An exact sign-flip permutation over the same pairs, which assumes nothing about the shape of the difference distribution, gives p=0.0001p=0.0001, 0.07840.0784, 0.00680.0068 and 0.00390.0039: the two survivors keep their place, and the 3.7B contrast joins them at an adjusted 0.034. The signed-rank test is the one registered in advance, so the confirmatory reading stays at two, and the 3.7B rung is reported as boundary evidence rather than as a third confirmed result. The other twelve contrasts in Table 5 use the same interval procedure and are reported as descriptive, because they were not among the four registered in advance rather than because anything about their baselines was chosen after the fact. The winner’s-curse argument belongs to the gap-to-best estimator of Section 4.3, which picks its comparator from this ladder’s results. The four baselines here are a fixed set.

Task by task, Mingbird beats goose on 14, 11 and 11 of the comparable tasks at 0.75B, 1.9B and 3.7B, and loses on 0, 3 and 1, so the mean gap is not the work of a few large wins. At 4.7B the two arms tie on eight tasks, every one of them at 1.000. Mingbird wins nine and loses one, HWF-13, where goose reaches 1.000 and Mingbird 0.857. The suite has saturated for this pair at the top of the ladder, which is the ceiling discussed in Section 4.3.

Two rungs, 0.75B and 4.7B, were collected a second time, which repeats the decisive contrasts on the same tasks (72 cells, of which the same infrastructure rule removes eight). At 4.7B the repeat is nearly exact. Mingbird scores 0.968 and then 0.988, goose 0.718 in the matrix and 0.731 in the repeat over the seventeen tasks it has in both. The paired gap is +0.250+0.250 [+0.107,+0.408][+0.107,+0.408] over the eighteen tasks both arms complete in the matrix and +0.256+0.256 [+0.105,+0.437][+0.105,+0.437] over the seventeen in the repeat, and fifteen of the eighteen Mingbird cells repeat their score to the digit. At 0.75B the level falls and the gap does not. On the ten tasks where both arms are clean in both collections Mingbird drops 0.156 and goose 0.01, and the paired gap is +0.420+0.420 and then +0.423+0.423. Over every usable cell Mingbird falls from 0.664 to 0.503 and goose from 0.186 to 0.154. The paired gap over the tasks both arms complete is +0.508+0.508 [+0.339,+0.682][+0.339,+0.682] and then +0.476+0.476 [+0.260,+0.701][+0.260,+0.701], fourteen wins and no losses the first time and nine and none the second. Those counts are over usable cells, and the exclusions matter to them: restoring the nine cells the rule removes at this rung, two in the matrix and seven in the repeat, gives fifteen wins and one loss in the matrix and twelve wins and two losses in the repeat, +0.466+0.466 [+0.249,+0.664][+0.249,+0.664] and +0.315+0.315 [+0.061,+0.541][+0.061,+0.541], because every one of the three losses is a cell on which one arm’s run was cut short by the server rather than by the model. Under both exclusion rules the contrast stays positive while its size moves. The level at the smallest rung is a draw from a wide distribution, the contrast is not.

The winner is not the arm that moves most. The precision ladder runs the published granite tag again as its unquantized level, which repeats the 3.7B cells for Mingbird and pi in a collection that ran at the matrix’s speed. pi falls from 0.714 to 0.493 there, a change larger than the winner’s at 0.75B, while Mingbird moves from 0.762 to 0.822 over the same eighteen cells. The repeats do not support a stable level for any arm, Mingbird included. They support a paired contrast that survives where both arms are measured again.

4.3 How the advantage changes with size

The next question is whether the harness matters more or less as the model grows. Figure 3 and Table 6 answer it with four estimators on one common task panel: the span across five harnesses, the span with the reply-contract arm removed, the gap to the pre-specified comparator, and the gap to whichever baseline is strongest at that rung.

On that panel the spans are 0.653, 0.601, 0.791 and 0.782 at the four rungs. They differ by up to 0.04 from Table 4 because the panel drops the three tasks that one arm is missing on. Their slope is +0.198+0.198 with an interval of [−0.078,+0.476][-0.078,+0.476], consistent with a rise of half a point per decade and with a fall of a tenth. The four-arm span, which drops the reply-contract floor, has no slope either (+0.011+0.011, [−0.302,+0.257][-0.302,+0.257]), and the pre-specified gap to goose does not resolve across the four rungs (−0.195-0.195, [−0.494,+0.100][-0.494,+0.100]).

Within the Qwen family alone that gap does resolve, at −0.332-0.332 with an interval of [−0.639,−0.025][-0.639,-0.025], and it is the one place in the paper where a within-family trend clears its interval. It is a level difference, not a trend: the three points are 0.508, 0.231 and 0.245, so the whole decline is the first step, off the rung where two baselines leave the task empty, and the last step goes the other way. A line through those three points is not a trend estimate, and the quadratic test does not prefer a curve to a line (p=0.572p=0.572), so neither shape is identified, and the estimate is reported in the table for completeness rather than as a slope.

One quantity does move. The margin over the best baseline at each rung is 0.461, 0.246, −0.061-0.061 and 0.071, a slope of −0.591-0.591 [−0.836,−0.251][-0.836,-0.251]. The decline measures the baselines rather than the harness. The best baseline at 0.75B is goose at 0.186. At the other three rungs it is pi. pi climbs from 0.172 to 0.893 across the ladder, a steeper trajectory than Mingbird’s 0.664 to 0.968, so the leader’s margin narrows while the spread among harnesses stays the same. A study that compared the winner only against the current champion would read that as leverage shrinking with scale. The spans, which hold the comparison set fixed, do not.

Two properties of the design set what the ends of the ladder can show. At 3.7B the cross-family model lets pi draw level: the gap to best is −0.061-0.061 on the common panel and the paired interval includes zero, so this rung is a tie at both readings. At 4.7B the suite saturates: on the full eighteen tasks, Mingbird and goose both reach 1.000 on eight of them, and on the table’s fifteen-task panel the count is six, where the goose gap is 0.262 against 0.436 on the nine tasks the pair does not both solve. Both are properties of the measurement rather than of the harnesses.

Taken together, the three artifacts give the ladder a specific limit. A floor arm that fails at every size manufactures a rise in the span. A ceiling at the top manufactures a decline in the winner’s margin. A single cross-family rung in the middle manufactures a peak. Each of the three has been read as a property of harness leverage, and each is reproducible here by choosing the estimator. The pattern is not specific to harnesses: whether a capability trend appears at all depends on the metric chosen to look for it (Schaeffer et al.,, 2023). What the ladder does establish is the level: at every rung the harnesses are separated by a margin the intervals resolve. What it cannot establish is the slope, and no arrangement of these four rungs would. A leverage-versus-size claim needs three things this ladder does not have: a baseline set with no floor arm, tasks that stay unsaturated at the top rung, and at least two model families at every rung, or a within-family slope alone.

4.4 What carries the advantage

The mechanism gradient repeats one harness with its completion controls switched off, at 0.75B, 1.9B, 3.7B and 4.7B, eighteen tasks per arm. Table 7 reports the three arms at each rung.

At 0.75B the full gate averages 0.431 and disabling the six executable checks costs 0.080, with a paired interval of [−0.183,+0.320][-0.183,+0.320] that includes zero. At 1.9B the same contrast is 0.117 [−0.047,+0.302][-0.047,+0.302]. At 4.7B it is −0.004-0.004 [−0.052,+0.044][-0.052,+0.044]: full 0.980, guards off 0.984. The ablation also runs at 3.7B, on granite, where the difference is +0.003+0.003 [−0.032,+0.038][-0.032,+0.038].

Set against the ladder, those numbers are small. The lead over goose is 0.508 at 0.75B, 0.221 at 1.9B, 0.484 at 3.7B and 0.250 at 4.7B. The point estimate of the gate’s contribution is therefore 16% of the lead at 0.75B, 53% at 1.9B, and under 2% at the two rungs above. The intervals bound the contribution tightly at the top: at 4.7B the upper limit is 0.044, or 18% of the lead. At 0.75B the upper limit is 0.320, so the interval cannot exclude a gate contribution of up to 63%. The point estimate is what places it near a sixth.

The failure coding shows where the gate does act. At 1.9B the full arm leaves no artifact on 0 of 18 tasks, the guards-off arm on 3, and the text-only arm on 1, so switching the checks off produces three empty runs that the full harness prevents. At 0.75B the count is 7, 6 and 6: there the checks do not change how often a run ends empty, and the 0.080 appears in partial scores instead. At 3.7B and 4.7B the counts are 1, 1, 1 and 0, 0, 0. Completion control does what it was designed to do at 1.9B. At 0.75B the gate is not what produces the 0.508 lead: its point estimate is a sixth of that and the interval admits up to 63%, and the empty-run count, which does not rise when the checks are switched off, is what places it outside the story there.

Where the rest of the lead comes from can be bounded from the other side. Split each paired gap by whether the baseline left any of its declared artifacts. At 0.75B, 8 of the 17 comparable pi cells are empty and they carry 51% of the gap to pi, 10 of 16 goose cells 68%, and 11 of 17 OpenCode cells 72%. The remainder is a difference on cells both arms completed, and it is large: Mingbird is +0.443+0.443 [+0.085,+0.714][+0.085,+0.714] ahead of pi and +0.439+0.439 [+0.248,+0.628][+0.248,+0.628] ahead of goose on the tasks those arms did produce. At 1.9B the balance shifts almost entirely to availability: the empty cells carry 94% of the gap to pi and 90% of the gap to goose, and on produced cells the gap is +0.016+0.016 [−0.261,+0.313][-0.261,+0.313] and +0.032+0.032 [−0.210,+0.246][-0.210,+0.246]. At 3.7B the pair with pi is level on the 16 tasks both arms complete (−0.057-0.057, [−0.267,+0.146][-0.267,+0.146]). At 4.7B the character reverses: pi leaves no empty cell, and the whole +0.075+0.075 [+0.012,+0.147][+0.012,+0.147] lead is a difference in how much of the task the two arms finish.

The advantage is therefore a progress effect at every rung: at the small end it is mostly a difference in whether a run gets anywhere, and at the top it is a difference in how far a completed run gets. The six checks produce neither. What must produce it is whatever keeps a weak model working after a tool error or inside a repetition loop, and the transcripts name one such process exactly.

At 0.75B, eleven of pi’s eighteen cells contain the shell’s answer to an unquoted Unix-rooted path, “cd: too many arguments”, and nine of those eleven end with nothing written. The tool surface explains where the command comes from: pi exposes read, bash, edit and write, so a model that wants to list a directory has to do it through the shell, and the shell is where a Unix-rooted path with a space fails. In HWF-02 the model then issues a directory-listing bash call 274 times, 273 of them byte-identical: the path fails on every turn, the error is appended to the context, and the request grows by 113 tokens a turn from 1,844 to 32,767, where the run stops. The same model on the same task in Mingbird scores 0.786, and Mingbird’s tools take the directory as a native call rather than a shell command. Its transcript records the repeated call disabled, ten further attempts, a context reset from 7,033 to 2,237 tokens, and then the artifact written and the task finished. Across the rung no Mingbird cell exceeds 29 identical calls and the intercept fires in all seventeen. Pi has twelve cells above 100 identical calls, goose eight and OpenCode four.

That is the process the decomposition’s empty-cell channel is made of: a single failing action repeated until the window fills. A harness that interrupts the repeat and resets the context converts the run. One that does not reaches the iteration cap with an empty directory. The completion gate sits outside this chain, which is why switching it off changes the empty-run count at 0.75B by one cell in the wrong direction.

One rule in that chain can be switched off alone. The build’s anti_loop ablation disables the streak rule, which blocks the same tool call eight times in a row and the same call signature four times, and leaves the read-loop intercept and the hard context reset in place. Eighteen tasks were run twice at 0.75B, full and streak-off, interleaved inside one batch. The full arm scores 0.411 higher on average, [+0.218,+0.608][+0.218,+0.608], higher on twelve tasks and lower on one. On eight tasks it is the only arm that writes any declared artifact, and the reverse never occurs. The switch is visible in the transcripts: the full arm’s eighteen cells record 253 calls to a tool the harness had already disabled, and the off arm’s record 55. The 55 are 45 todo calls and 10 web calls, and no file tool is among them, because what survives the switch belongs to the todo and web rules it does not touch. The point estimate sits close to what a rerun moves a Mingbird cell by at this rung (0.37 on average), and one run per cell cannot separate a 0.411 mean from that noise. The artifact split is a separate observation, and it is the one repeated runs would have to close: eight tasks produce a declared artifact in the full arm and none in the off arm, no task goes the other way, and a two-sided sign test over those eight disagreements gives p=0.0078p=0.0078, conditional on the eight and treating tasks as independent.

The process changes with rung, and the counts say how. At 1.9B none of pi’s five empty cells ends normally: four reach the wall budget and one stalls, so the availability channel there is time rather than repetition. Rescoring those cells’ working directories lifts pi by 0.143 and Mingbird by 0.139, which leaves that rung’s contrast at +0.180+0.180 [−0.006,+0.371][-0.006,+0.371]: the gap is not an artifact of scoring a timeout as zero. At 3.7B nine of OpenCode’s twelve empty cells and eight of goose’s nine are budget timeouts. At 4.7B mini-swe-agent accounts for 13 of the 16 empty cells, and ten of its thirteen end normally on its reply contract.

The todo-sync reminder is the one intervention switched off in the text-only arm and on in both others, so it owns the second contrast. It moves without a consistent sign: −0.035-0.035 at 0.75B, −0.079-0.079 at 1.9B, +0.095+0.095 at 3.7B and −0.016-0.016 at 4.7B. The arms reorder as well: the text-only arm is the lowest at 3.7B, 0.812 against 0.910 for the full gate, and the highest at 4.7B, 1.000 against 0.980. The 3.7B difference is a level in one collection, and the repeat collection does not reproduce it.

The slope of the guard contribution on log10\log_{10} size is −0.104-0.104 with an interval of [−0.414,+0.220][-0.414,+0.220] and a bootstrap p=0.525p=0.525. The contribution grows or shrinks with size by no amount this design can resolve: it is small and positive at the two small rungs, zero at the two large ones, and the family’s adjusted pp for the slope is 1.000.

The gradient’s full arm is a second collection of the matrix’s Mingbird cell, which measures how far an arm mean moves between collections. The two agree at 4.7B (0.980 against 0.968) and diverge at the small rungs: 0.431 against 0.664 at 0.75B, 0.822 against 0.593 at 1.9B, and 0.910 against 0.762 at 3.7B. The spread is bimodal, the same shape the 72-cell replication shows: most tasks repeat their score exactly and a few move by most of the scale. The gradient measures one arm, not a contrast, so it cannot carry an ordering claim across collections. It carries the size of the drift: 0.229 at 1.9B between two collections of the same configuration, which is the scale against which every level in this paper is read. The ordering claim rests instead on the matrix and on the repeat that contains both arms, in Section 4.2.

The 3.7B rung is where that instability is largest in absolute terms. A repeat of the whole 3.7B gradient puts the full arm at 0.844 against 0.910, and the guard contrast at −0.020-0.020 against +0.003+0.003. Across the two collections the contrast is zero either way. At the three Qwen rungs the gradient’s contrasts are paired within one collection and never compared across collections, and they carry intervals because a difference of that size is near what eighteen paired tasks can resolve.

4.5 How small models fail

Each cell is coded on two axes, from its working directory and its runner record rather than from the transcript. The artifact axis records whether all, some, or none of the declared artifacts exist. The termination axis records how the run ended: finished, wall budget, a no-artifact exit in which the harness reported completion with nothing written, stall, early finish, or an error exit in which the harness process returned nonzero. The two axes are independent and keeping them apart matters, because a cell can finish with no artifacts and a cell can be stopped with all of them. Cells whose failure is infrastructure and not agent behavior are excluded by the rule in Section 6 and re-run.

Table 8 and Figure 4 aggregate the coding over the 357 usable ladder cells. Of the 127 cells that produce none of their declared artifacts, 85 end with a normal runner exit and 29 hit the wall budget. A harness can therefore fail a task while its process reports success, which is why the artifact axis is coded from the working directory rather than from an exit code. The rate ranges from 4 of 70 cells for Mingbird to 50 of 72 for mini-swe-agent, with pi at 15 of 72, goose at 26 of 71 and OpenCode at 32 of 72.

The share is rung-dependent. At 0.75B nearly all artifact-free cells end normally, 43 of 48. At 1.9B the share falls to 19 of 33, and at 3.7B only 10 of 30 do, because there the no-artifact cells mostly run to the wall budget: 20 of the 30, of which nine are OpenCode cells and eight goose cells. At 4.7B the quiet stop returns: 13 of 16 artifact-free cells end normally, and ten of those 13 belong to mini-swe-agent.

The 85 normal exits are not all quiet in the same sense, and a third pass over the transcripts, separate from the two-axis coding, says which are. A cell is error-bearing when its transcript records a traceback, an explicit error line, a repeated-format error or a parse error, with terminal color codes stripped first. The quiet stop is concentrated in two arms: 14 of pi’s 15 artifact-free cells record no line matching those patterns, and 22 of OpenCode’s 32 do not. Nine of pi’s fifteen empty cells and nine of OpenCode’s thirty-two carry the shell’s “cd: too many arguments” as ordinary tool output, which the patterns do not treat as an error because the harness passes the message through instead of raising it, so a clean transcript is not a clean run. What the coding measures is whether the harness reported a failure, not whether one occurred. goose sits between them, at 18 of its 26 artifact-free cells recording no error line. mini-swe-agent is the opposite extreme: 40 of its 50 artifact-free cells carry an error line, and 34 of them carry its own RepeatedFormatError, so that arm usually stops on a named contract rather than silently. Mingbird leaves four artifact-free cells, all of which end normally and all four of which record an error line in the transcript.

The distinction sets what a scoring rule can and cannot substitute for. A rule that read a normal process exit as completion would credit 85 runs that wrote none of their declared artifacts, and 40 of them would carry no error line in the transcript as well. The arms share an exit status that does not record the failure, rather than a process that fails.

Three failure shapes recur. At 0.75B, pi’s and OpenCode’s zero cells are dominated by a host mismatch: the model emits an unquoted Unix path, the shell answers “cd: too many arguments”, and the working directory stays empty. pi records that error in eleven of its eighteen cells and OpenCode in six. Neither Mingbird nor goose nor mini-swe-agent records it at that rung, and OpenCode records it in nine cells across the other three rungs. mini-swe-agent fails by a second route, because its loop requires a bash block in every reply and a model that repeats a non-conforming reply ends the run with the harness’s own RepeatedFormatError. That status appears in fifteen of eighteen cells at 0.75B, fifteen at 1.9B, none at 3.7B and sixteen at 4.7B. At 3.7B the format error disappears and the same harness reaches the wall budget in five of its eighteen cells, so its failures there are neither a reply-contract failure nor predominantly a speed failure. That rung is the cross-family point, so the change tracks the family, not the size.

Repetition is the second failure shape. In many cells the agent repeats one action verbatim until the cell ends: at 0.75B the median cell’s longest run of identical calls is 272 for pi and 36.5 for OpenCode against 21 for Mingbird, and pi’s longest run in one cell reaches 273. At 1.9B the medians are 63.5 and 2.5 against 21. Mingbird repeats as well, but its transcript records an explicit duplicate-call intercept and its runs stay in the tens, not in the hundreds. Pooling the three CLI baselines within a rung, cells whose longest run reaches ten calls average 0.09, 0.25, 0.01 and 0.55 at the four rungs, against 0.27, 0.44, 0.45 and 0.83 for the cells below that threshold. The relation is a correlation, not a treatment effect, because the harder tasks produce both longer runs and lower scores.

The third shape concerns what a score means. The scorer reads structure and fixture strings, not provenance, so a fluent artifact can pass with invented citations. On HWF-01, the one task whose fixture supplies external DOIs, we audited every DOI in the produced artifacts against the eighteen records the fixture ships. At 0.75B, pi’s artifact carries those eighteen DOIs and no others. Mingbird’s carries twenty-eight distinct DOIs, of which six appear in the fixture, so twenty-two are invented. Both cells score 1.000. The scorer never reads a DOI, and on this cell its verdict cannot distinguish the two. The audit therefore bounds what a high score means for a small model without contradicting any score here. An artifact that names the right files and sections can still carry four invented identifiers for every one it quotes.

A blind audit of sixty cells by two reviewers puts a number on that depth. Their mean judgment correlates with the checker at 0.57 (p<0.001p<0.001), and on the thirty-four cells the checker scores 1.000 both reviewers independently mark the content wrong in eight. A high score here is conformance to the specification, not correctness of the work.

4.6 Cost and the upper anchor

Every cell records its wall clock. The five arms share one server that executes a single request at a time, so the elapsed time of a rung is a fraction of its total and GPU occupancy is lower still.

The whole 0.75B rung cost 6.1 agent-hours for ninety cells, the 1.9B rung 9.6, 3.7B 19.4 and 4.7B 6.5. Per-cell time and score do not travel together: at 0.75B OpenCode has the shortest mean cell at 2.4 minutes and one of the lowest scores, and at 4.7B the five arms finish within a minute of each other.

Per-cell minutes hide the cost that decides a deployment, which is the time spent per artifact set actually delivered. Table 9 divides each arm’s total time in a rung by its number of complete artifact sets. At 3.7B OpenCode needs 195 minutes per complete set against the winner’s six, a factor of thirty-two, although its per-cell mean is only four times longer. At 0.75B it never produces a set at all, and the arm that spends the least time per cell there is the one that finishes nothing. The winner is also the cheapest arm per delivered set at all four rungs, and the others do not keep their score order: at 1.9B pi is second by score and slowest of the four arms that deliver a set, while goose is second by cost there and third by score.

The 35.5B anchor bounds the measurement at the top instead of extending the ladder. Both arms were run on all eighteen tasks, 36 cells in total, and the anchor is reported on the six cheapest, chosen as the ones with the fewest deliverables. goose solves all six and averages 1.000. Mingbird solves five and averages 0.833, because one cell reaches its budget. Over all eighteen tasks the two arms average 0.952 and 0.944, and the paired difference on the six tasks is −0.167-0.167 with an interval of [−0.500,0.000][-0.500,0.000], which is not separable from zero at six tasks. The anchor shows the ceiling: at 35.5B one harness solves the cheapest six outright and the other is one budget short, so the task set has a defined upper working range. The wall clock says the same thing from the other side: goose spends 40.0 minutes over the six cells and Mingbird 95.8, with the longest cell 10.0 minutes against 45.0. Those minutes come from the hardware rather than the harness. Only a quarter of the model’s weights fit in the card at this context (5.5 of 22.6 GB), so most of the inference runs on the CPU and the anchor’s wall clock is not comparable to the ladder’s. A subset chosen for runtime is a subset chosen for ease, and the anchor is reported as a bound on the measurement, not as evidence that harness differences vanish at the top of the ladder. In the earlier matrix the 4.7B Qwen outscored this model over the same eighteen tasks (Wang and Huang,, 2026), and that ordering does not survive on the six cheapest tasks.

4.7 Precision

The ladder above changes the model and holds the harness fixed. It does not hold precision fixed, and Section 6 states the consequence: the two smallest Qwen tags ship at Q8_0 and the rest at Q4_K_M, so a size comparison across 1.9B also crosses a bit-width change, and the sign of that change cannot be read from the ladder because a wider model and a better-quantized one move in the same direction. The interaction is known from the quantization literature, where bit width and parameter count trade off against each other and the trade-off is not linear (Dettmers and Zettlemoyer,, 2023; Kumar et al.,, 2024).

To measure it we ran a precision ladder on a single base model at four bit widths: granite4.2:3b at q2_K (3.15 bits per weight), q3_K_S (3.63), Q4_K_M (4.85) and q6_K (6.50). Bits per weight are computed from each served artifact’s byte count and parameter count, not from the label, because a K-quant carries more bits than its name suggests. Every level runs the same 18 tasks with the same two arms and the same protocol as the ladder above: temperature zero, thinking disabled, a 32K window, and the per-tier budgets of Section 3. The arms are Mingbird and pi, the baseline that is strongest at three of the ladder’s four rungs.

The levels are ordered so that every task meets all four bit widths back to back. Collected level by level, the four would be weeks apart, and a level collected after a reboot would differ from one collected before it for reasons that have nothing to do with precision. Ordering by task makes each of the four comparisons a within-task contrast, and the arm and level orders both reverse by task parity, so neither position nor warm-up systematically favors one side. Every level mean reported here therefore comes from one contiguous, task-interleaved collection.

The hypothesis registered for this axis is that the harness advantage over the baseline grows as precision falls. The tests are four paired contrasts, one per level, plus one slope of the contrast against bits per weight. Tasks that both arms solve at a level are dropped before the contrast, so a ceiling cannot produce a trend, and where the desaturated and raw readings differ the desaturated one governs. A level on which every arm scored zero would be a collapse point and would leave the fit. None of the four reaches that state, so all four enter it. The family is Holm-corrected separately from the confirmatory family above, and all five tests stay in it. After correction only the slope survives, at adjusted p=0.048p=0.048, and the three level contrasts rise to 0.057. The lowest level yields only two non-zero pairs, too few for a rank test, so its contrast carries p=1p=1 rather than being dropped: removing a test from a pre-registered family after seeing the data is the one move the correction exists to prevent. It stays in the table as well, because a collapse is a result.

Table 10 reports the four levels. Under the deployment reading, which is the paper’s primary one, the advantage does not grow as precision falls. It is largest at 4.85 bits, where Mingbird averages 0.822 against pi’s 0.493, a gap of +0.329+0.329 with an interval of [+0.131,+0.544][+0.131,+0.544]. At 6.50 bits it is +0.292+0.292 [+0.099,+0.503][+0.099,+0.503], and at 3.63 bits +0.264+0.264 [+0.094,+0.437][+0.094,+0.437]. Both intervals exclude zero. At 3.15 bits Mingbird averages 0.029 from fourteen completed cells and pi’s mean is zero because every one of its cells reached its budget. The gap is +0.029+0.029 [+0.000,+0.075][+0.000,+0.075].

The registered hypothesis, that the harness advantage widens as precision falls, is contradicted under the deployment reading and undecided under the rescored one. The gap between the two readings is itself the result: at high precision the baseline’s deficit is time rather than quality.

Fitted across the four levels on the desaturated contrasts, the slope of the gap against bits per weight is +0.139+0.139 with an interval of [+0.037,+0.235][+0.037,+0.235] and a bootstrap p=0.010p=0.010. The preregistered direction was negative, a gap that widens as precision falls. The estimate is positive and its interval excludes zero, so under the deployment reading the registered hypothesis is contradicted rather than undecided. Under the Holm correction over all five tests the slope is the one member of the family to survive (adjusted p=0.048p=0.048). The three level contrasts follow at 0.0570.057 each and the untestable level at 1, so the levels are not significant on their own. The sign is not carried by the collapse point: dropping the 3.15-bit level makes the estimate more positive.

The rescored block of Table 10 takes each of the forty-one cells that reached its budget and scores the working directory it left behind. It moves the two high-precision levels and little else. At 4.85 bits pi’s mean rises from 0.493 to 0.854 and the gap falls from +0.329+0.329 to +0.023+0.023, interval [−0.167,+0.203][-0.167,+0.203]. At 6.50 bits pi rises from 0.568 to 0.855 and the gap falls from +0.292+0.292 to +0.004+0.004, interval [−0.162,+0.180][-0.162,+0.180]. At 3.63 bits pi’s mean is unchanged and the gap stays +0.264+0.264 [+0.100,+0.439][+0.100,+0.439]. At 3.15 bits pi’s rescored mean rises to 0.029 and the gap is zero to three decimals.

So the contradiction of the registered precision hypothesis belongs to the deployment reading, and the section does not read it as a statement about the systems alone. Fitted to the rescored gaps the slope is −0.030-0.030 with an interval of [−0.152,+0.098][-0.152,+0.098], which is indistinguishable from zero: if the work already on disk when the run was stopped counts, this design cannot order the levels at all. What holds under both readings is smaller and still useful. At 3.15 bits both arms collapse to near-zero scores: Mingbird keeps a mean of 0.029 from the fourteen cells it finishes, while every pi cell reaches its budget. At 3.63 bits both produce work but at a fraction of their higher-precision scores, 0.458 and 0.195. Between 4.85 and 6.50 bits pi’s deficit is a deficit of time and not of quality, since its timed-out cells were completing most of the task. That is the signature the rescored reading is built to measure.

The arms also fail differently at every level. At 6.50 bits pi reaches its budget in seven of eighteen cells and Mingbird in none. At 4.85 bits eight of pi’s eighteen reach it, against one Mingbird timeout and one cell that exits on an error in the harness. At 3.63 bits six of pi’s cells reach it and one stalls, against none for Mingbird. At 3.15 bits all eighteen of pi’s cells reach it while Mingbird finishes fourteen and produces no artifact in three. A timeout scores zero under the deployment reading, so part of the low-end gap measures whether work finishes at all rather than how well it is done. Cells that reached the budget stay in the denominator, scored zero, which is the deployment rule used everywhere else in the paper.

The four levels are four quantizations of one checkpoint, all official GGUF files downloaded from the publisher rather than re-quantized here, so no level is a second compression of another. The base model is granite 4.2 3B, the only family in the study served with a full range of bit widths: the 4.7B family ships at two levels, which cannot carry a four-level ladder. The top level is Q6_K rather than Q8_0 because at a 32K window Q8_0 holds 6.28 of its 6.76 GB in VRAM and would have measured memory placement alongside bit width. The comparator is pi, the stronger baseline at 3.7B (0.714 against goose’s 0.262), so the contrast is if anything harder than one against goose. The ladder is therefore a within-family measurement: four quantizations of one checkpoint at one rung, and its result does not transfer to another rung by construction. It ran on the successor host of B.

Read as a measurement of the caveat rather than as a trend, the pattern is that compression costs the two arms different things. Going from 6.50 to 4.85 bits costs pi 0.075 under the deployment reading and Mingbird 0.038. At 3.63 bits both fall to a fraction of their high-precision scores and at 3.15 bits both reach zero. The ladder does not support the claim that the margin is larger where deployments actually run: under the deployment reading it is, and under the rescored reading it is not, because the baseline’s losses at those levels are work already on disk when the budget ran out rather than work that never existed. A reader on a fixed overnight schedule should read the harness choice at high precision as a choice about score. A reader who can wait for late work should read it as a choice about time.

5 Discussion

Harness choice sets the level at every size

The result a practitioner can act on is the level, and it is the same result at every rung. Mingbird is first at 0.75B, 1.9B, 3.7B and 4.7B. Of the four pre-registered rung contrasts two survive Holm correction, at 0.75B (adjusted p=0.0067p=0.0067) and 4.7B (0.04100.0410), and two do not. Thirteen of the sixteen paired comparisons exclude zero overall, and the leads that do run from 0.075 over the strongest rival at 4.7B to 0.819 over the weakest. A single rung’s level is not a stable object: the 0.75B winner averages 0.664, 0.503 and 0.431 in three collections, and the same arm at granite averages 0.762 in the matrix and 0.822 in the precision ladder. The ordering is steadier than the level, but only for the pair that was repeated: Mingbird and goose were re-collected at 0.75B and 4.7B and Mingbird leads both times, while pi, OpenCode and mini-swe-agent were run once and their levels rest on a single collection. A team that owns one 8 GB card should choose the harness with as much care as the model, and should not expect a larger model to repair a bad one: at 4.7B the four baselines still sit 0.075 to 0.819 below the winner.

The slope is not measurable with four rungs

Two published predictions disagree about the direction of the interaction, one expecting the strongest model to gain most from scaffolding and one expecting the gains to shrink as capability rises. This ladder cannot settle the disagreement, and it shows why the disagreement is hard to settle at all. Three artifacts each produce a direction. A floor arm that fails at every size inflates the span into a rise. A ceiling at 4.7B, where Mingbird and pi both score 1.000 on eleven of the eighteen tasks, compresses the winner’s margin into a decline. A single cross-family rung at 3.7B puts a peak in the middle. Each of the three has been read as a property of harness leverage, and each is reproducible here by choosing the estimator. A design that could resolve the slope needs tasks that stay unsaturated at the top and a baseline set with no floor arm. That is a different suite, not a longer run of this one.

What the ablation rules out

The paper’s design hypothesis was that the six executable checks would carry the advantage. The ablation says otherwise at three of the four rungs. All six together are worth 0.080 at 0.75B and 0.117 at 1.9B, with intervals that include zero, and nothing at 3.7B and 4.7B. At the smallest rung the point estimate is a sixth of the 0.508 lead. The gate does do its job where the model stops leaving work: at 1.9B, switching it off turns 0 empty runs into 3. At 0.75B it changes neither the number of empty runs nor much of the score, so the 0.080 appears in partial credit rather than in saved runs.

The lead is a progress effect. At 0.75B between half and three quarters of each gap is cells the baseline left empty, and most of the rest is a depth difference on tasks both arms completed. At 1.9B almost all of it is availability. Against pi at 4.7B, where no cell is empty, all of it is depth on tasks both arms finish. The transcripts show the process behind the availability part: at 0.75B nine of pi’s empty cells end in one failing shell command repeated until the 32K window fills. We name this the repeat-until-window-full failure. The same model completes the task in Mingbird after the repeat is interrupted and the context reset. At 0.75B the dominant failure is not wrong work but unbounded repetition of one failing action. A harness that bounds repetition turns empty runs into completed ones, and the completion gate is orthogonal to that channel. The machinery that bounds it is what the completion gradient does not touch: a tool surface that takes the directory as a call rather than a shell string, a prompt that states the platform and the paths, loop and context guards, and compaction that keeps the window usable. One piece of it can be switched off alone, and the test is not subtle: without the streak rule the score falls by 0.411 at 0.75B and eight of eighteen tasks lose their artifact altogether. Those are the parts to replicate. A completion gate is cheap and harmless, and it is the right response to a model that cannot recognize its own incomplete work, but a study that measured only the gate would report a small effect and could conclude, wrongly, that harnesses do not matter.

The failure to design against is the quiet stop

Exit status, the transcript’s error line and the artifact state are three signals that do not substitute for one another, and a failure gets harder to see the further back the scorer looks. A benchmark that scores crashes will rate an agent highly while it produces nothing, because the typical failure of a small model is a normal exit with an empty working directory. Of the 127 empty cells, 85 end normally and 40 of those carry no error line at all. This changes what an evaluation should measure. Artifact state at the end of a run is the outcome of interest, and the process exit is not. It also changes what a harness should do. A stop rule that trusts the model’s claim of completion is a stop rule optimized for a model that is usually right, which is not the model in front of it.

The cost of getting this wrong is asymmetric. A harness that stops too early loses the whole task. A harness that stops too late loses time, and time is what the budget measures. Completion control buys the first against the second, and the price is visible in the cost numbers: at 1.9B Mingbird spends 4.2 minutes per cell more than OpenCode and earns nine more complete artifact sets.

What the upper anchor does and does not show

At 35.5B goose saturates the six-task subset and Mingbird is one budget short of it, so at that size the suite has no resolution left for one arm while the other stops just short of the ceiling. That is a property of the measurement, not a finding about large models. A ceiling anchor that covers only the cheapest tasks cannot say whether harness differences persist at scale. It does say that the task set has a defined upper working range, which is useful information for anyone reusing it.

Relation to the Mingbird system paper

The preprint (Wang and Huang,, 2026) describes Mingbird as an architecture: its components, its seven design principles, its completion-control mechanism, and a 288-cell development matrix over four models from 2B to 35B. This paper treats the same harness as one of five arms and asks a different question, which is how the choice of harness compares across model sizes. How Mingbird is built is described there, and what it is worth against four alternatives at four sizes is measured here.

6 Threats to validity

Construct validity

The outcome is artifact completion on 18 tasks scored by a deterministic checker. That is a narrow slice of what practitioners want from an agent. It rewards a working directory that satisfies a written specification and says nothing about code review, maintainability, or the quality of the reasoning that produced it. The prompt states which files are expected and which checks will run, so the tasks measure specification following. The checks are shallow by construction, since they test for named files, required sections, and values quoted from the fixtures. A hollow artifact that names the right things can pass, and Section 4.5 measures this on HWF-01, where 22 of the 28 distinct DOIs in one artifact were invented while the task still scored 1.000. A deterministic checker is a partial oracle in the sense the software-testing literature gives that term (Barr et al.,, 2015): it decides the cases it can decide and is silent about the rest, and a study built on one inherits exactly that limit. The instrument properties reported in Section 3 are the ones the current checklist for agentic benchmarks asks for (Zhu et al.,, 2025). The checker was audited against blind human scores. Sixty cells were drawn at random from this collection, from the 202 whose declared artifacts were still on disk to show reviewers, 230 having produced at least one at collection time, and two reviewers scored each for completeness, correctness and use of evidence. Their quadratic-weighted agreement runs from κ=0.58\kappa=0.58 to 0.690.69, and their mean correlates with the checker at 0.57 (permutation p<0.001p<0.001). What the correlation does not repair is the depth of the check.
